{{Short description|Geometric shape}}
[[File:Geometric_lemon.jpg |thumb|A lemon]]

In [[geometry]], a '''lemon''' is a [[geometric shape]] that is constructed as the [[surface of revolution]] of a [[circular arc]] of [[angle]] less than half of a full circle rotated about an axis passing through the endpoints of the lens (or arc). The surface of revolution of the complementary arc of the same circle, through the same axis, is called an '''apple'''.
[[File:spindle_torus_apple_lemon.png|thumb|An ''apple'' and a ''lemon'' derived from a [[torus#Geometry|spindle torus]] with proportions of a [[vesica piscis]] ]]
<!-- [[File:Standard_torus-spindle.png|thumb|right|Half of a self-intersecting torus]] -->
The apple and lemon together make up a '''spindle [[torus]]''' (or ''self-crossing torus'' or ''self-intersecting torus''). The lemon forms the boundary of a [[convex set]], while its surrounding apple is non-convex.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Kripac | first = Jiri
 | date = February 1997
 | doi = 10.1016/s0010-4485(96)00040-1
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Computer-Aided Design
 | pages = 113–122
 | title = A mechanism for persistently naming topological entities in history-based parametric solid models
 | volume = 29}}</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Krivoshapko | first1 = S. N.
 | last2 = Ivanov | first2 = V. N.
 | contribution = Surfaces of Revolution
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-11773-7_2
 | pages = 99–158
 | publisher = Springer International Publishing
 | title = Encyclopedia of Analytical Surfaces
 | year = 2015}}</ref>

[[File:CFL football.jpg|thumb|North American football]]
The ball in North American [[Gridiron_football|football]] has a shape resembling a geometric lemon. However, although used with a related meaning in geometry, the term "football" is more commonly used to refer to a surface of revolution whose [[Gaussian curvature]] is positive and [[constant curvature|constant]], formed from a more complicated curve than a circular arc.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Coombes | first1 = Kevin R.
 | last2 = Lipsman | first2 = Ronald L.
 | last3 = Rosenberg | first3 = Jonathan M.
 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4612-1698-8
 | page = 128
 | publisher = Springer New York
 | title = Multivariable Calculus and Mathematica
 | year = 1998| isbn = 978-0-387-98360-8
 }}</ref> Alternatively, a football may refer to a more abstract [[orbifold]], a surface modeled locally on a [[sphere]] except at two points.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Borzellino | first = Joseph E.
 | doi = 10.1017/S0004972700016464
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Bulletin of the Australian Mathematical Society
 | mr = 1274515
 | pages = 353–364
 | title = Pinching theorems for teardrops and footballs of revolution
 | volume = 49
 | year = 1994| doi-access = free
 }}</ref>

== Area and volume ==
The lemon is generated by rotating an arc of radius <math>R</math> and half-angle <math>\varphi_m</math> less than <math>\pi/2</math> about its chord.  Note that <math>\varphi</math> denotes latitude, as used in geophysics. The surface area is given by<ref>{{citation |last1=Verrall |first1=Steven C. |last2=Atkins |first2=Micah |last3=Kaminsky |first3=Andrew |last4=Friederick |first4=Emily |last5=Otto |first5=Andrew |last6=Verrall |first6=Kelly S. |last7=Lynch |first7=Peter |date=2023-01-23 |title=Ground State Quantum Vortex Proton Model |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10701-023-00669-y |journal=Foundations of Physics |language=en |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=28 |doi=10.1007/s10701-023-00669-y |s2cid=256115776 |issn=1572-9516|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
<math display="block">
 A = 2\pi R^2 \int_{-\varphi_m}^{\varphi_m} (\cos\varphi - \cos\varphi_m)\,d\varphi.
</math>

The volume is given by
<math display="block">
 V = \pi R^3 \int_{-\varphi_m}^{\varphi_m} (\cos\varphi - \cos\varphi_m)^2 \cos\varphi \,d\varphi.
</math>

These integrals can be evaluated analytically, giving
<math display="block">
 A = 4\pi R^2 (\sin\varphi_m - \varphi_m\cos\varphi_m),
</math>
<math display="block">
 V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \left[\sin^3\varphi_m - \tfrac{3}{4} \cos\varphi_m(2\varphi_m - \sin2\varphi_m)\right].
</math>

The apple is generated by rotating an arc of half-angle <math>\varphi_m</math> greater than <math>\pi/2</math> about its chord. The above equations are valid for both the lemon and apple.
